entry: Genus of mammals, the goats, in the family [[Bovidae]]. It comprises 10 species, including the markhor and several ibexes; nine wild species are usually accepted along with the domestic goat, *Capra hircus*. Wild goats live in mountain habitats, where they climb bare rock and survive on sparse vegetation. The domestic goat descends from the bezoar ibex (*Capra aegagrus aegagrus*) and is one of the oldest [[Domestication|domesticated]] species; domestication began at least 10,000 years ago in what is now northern Iran. Easy access to goat hair, meat and milk was the primary motivation, and goatskins were used for water and wine bottles and, in some regions, as [[Parchment|parchment]] until the [[Middle Ages]].

Pungent toxin that is the main active component of [[Chili pepper|chili peppers]]. It is a potent irritant for mammals, producing a burning sensation in any tissue it contacts; plants likely produce it as a deterrent against mammals and fungi. Pure capsaicin is a hydrophobic, crystalline solid. It activates the TRPV1 receptor in mammalian sensory neurons, but birds do not respond to it, a difference that may aid seed dispersal by birds. It adds heat to foods such as hot sauces and is used as a topical [[Analgesic|analgesic]] in creams and patches for neuropathic pain.

Fictional superhero in American comic books published by [[Marvel Comics]]. Created by Joe Simon and [[Jack Kirby]] as an explicitly anti-Nazi figure, he first appeared in *Captain America Comics* in December 1940. Steve Rogers, a frail man, is enhanced by a super-soldier serum and fights the [[Axis powers]] during [[World War II]]. Frozen in the war's final days, he is revived in modern times and becomes a leader of the Avengers. Political messages have remained a defining feature of the character's more than 10,000 stories. He has been portrayed by Chris Evans in the [[Marvel Cinematic Universe]].

[[New World monkey|New World monkeys]] of the subfamily *Cebinae*. Capuchins are known for complex foraging skills, such as using tools to crack open nuts, and have the largest brain-to-body ratio of any nonhuman primate. Their range extends through tropical forests from [[Central America]] to northern Argentina, and in [[Brazil]] they are called *macaco-prego* (nail monkey). The name derives from the Capuchin friars, whose brown robes and hoods the monkeys' coloring resembled. Classification is disputed. Some primatologists place the robust capuchins in *Sapajus*, separate from the gracile capuchins in *Cebus*; genetic studies date their divergence to about 6.2 million years ago. Capuchins are frequent victims of illegal wildlife trafficking, which is increasing.

Largest living [[Rodent|rodent]], a semiaquatic [[Herbivore|herbivore]] native to [[South America]] except Chile. It inhabits [[Savanna|savannas]] and dense forests near fresh water and feeds mainly on grasses and aquatic plants. Its close relatives include guinea pigs and rock cavies, and together with the lesser capybara it forms the genus *Hydrochoerus*. Capybaras are highly social, usually living in groups of 10–20 individuals but sometimes in groups as large as 100. Adults measure 106–134 cm in length and typically weigh 35–66 kg. They are hunted for meat, hide and the grease from their thick skin. The greater capybara, *Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris*, is classified as least concern by the IUCN.

Medium-sized wild [[Cat|cat]] native to [[Africa]], the [[Middle East]], [[Central Asia]] and arid areas of Pakistan and northwestern India. Typically nocturnal and secretive, it lives mainly alone or in pairs. It preys on birds, [[Rodent|rodents]] and other small mammals, and can leap higher than 3.0 m (9.8 ft) to catch birds in midair. Adults weigh 8–19 kg and stand 40–50 cm at the shoulder. Gestation lasts two to three months, and litters contain one to six kittens.

[[Roman emperor]] (r. 198–217). Elder son of Emperor Septimius Severus and a member of the Severan dynasty, he was proclaimed co-ruler with his father in 198. After having his brother Geta murdered in 211, he ruled alone. He issued the *Constitutio Antoniniana*, which extended Roman citizenship to all free inhabitants of the [[Roman Empire]] and gave the newly enfranchised men the name [[Marcus Aurelius]]. He began a campaign against the [[Parthian Empire]] in 216 but was assassinated in 217. Ancient sources portray him as a cruel tyrant.

Capital and largest city of [[Venezuela]]. Founded in 1567 as Santiago de León de Caracas, it lies in a valley of the coastal mountain range, separated from the [[Caribbean Sea]] by Cerro El Ávila, a mountain 2,200 meters (7,200 feet) high. The Caracas Stock Exchange and Petróleos de Venezuela (PDVSA) are headquartered in the city, and its historic center is generally considered to be the Caracas Cathedral on Bolívar Square. Caracas has some of the tallest skyscrapers in Latin America, including the Parque Central Towers. Since the early 2000s it has faced economic crisis, including hyperinflation exceeding 1,000,000% in 2018 and large-scale emigration.

[[Pre-Columbian era|Pre-Columbian]] society of north-central coastal [[Peru]]. Also called Norte Chico, it included as many as 30 major population centers in the Fortaleza, Pativilca and Supe river valleys. Its first city, Huaricanga, is generally dated to around 3500 BCE, and the civilization flourished between the 4th and 2nd millennia BCE before declining around 1800 BCE. Since the early 21st century it has been recognized as the oldest known civilization in the Americas and one of six places where civilization arose independently in the ancient world. It developed about a millennium after [[Sumer]]. It lacked ceramics and produced no surviving visual art; its monumental architecture included platform mounds and sunken circular plazas. Its namesake site, Caral, has six large [[Pyramid|pyramids]].

Italian painter, active mainly in [[Rome]]. Trained in [[Milan]], he moved to Rome in his twenties and became known for his violent, provocative behavior as well as his art. He worked rapidly from live models, painting directly on the canvas, and used a dramatic chiaroscuro known as tenebrism to depict violent struggles, torture and death. His realism and use of light had a formative influence on the [[Baroque]] style. After killing a man in a brawl, he was sentenced to death and fled to [[Naples]], then traveled to [[Malta]] and [[Sicily]]. He died in uncertain circumstances on the way from Naples to Rome, possibly of fever. Interest in his work revived in the 20th century.

Colorless, odorless, poisonous and flammable gas, CO, consisting of one carbon atom and one oxygen atom joined by a triple bond. It is the simplest carbon oxide, produced by the partial [[Combustion|combustion]] of carbon-containing fuels in [[Stove|stoves]], heating systems and vehicles. It is one of the most acutely toxic indoor air contaminants, and carbon monoxide poisoning is the most common type of fatal air poisoning in many countries. CO binds to [[Hemoglobin|hemoglobin]] approximately 200–250 times more strongly than oxygen, forming carboxyhemoglobin and impairing oxygen delivery. In mammals, low concentrations act as an endogenous [[Neurotransmitter|neurotransmitter]]. Industrially, it is used in producing drugs, fragrances and fuels, and as a reducing agent in [[Smelting|smelting]] iron ore.

Cylindrical allotrope of carbon with a diameter on the nanometer scale. Single-walled nanotubes (SWCNTs) have diameters of about 0.5–2.0 nanometers and can be idealized as a [[Graphene|graphene]] sheet rolled into a hollow cylinder. Multi-walled nanotubes (MWCNTs) consist of nested tubes with layers about 0.34 nanometers apart, as in [[Graphite|graphite]]. Some SWCNTs are metallic conductors and others are [[Semiconductor|semiconductors]]. Their tensile strength approaches 200 gigapascals, and their [[Young's modulus]] is about 1 TPa, comparable to diamond. Thermal conductivity exceeds 3000 W/m·K along the tube axis. SWCNTs were first synthesized in 1993, when researchers at NEC and [[IBM]] found that co-vaporizing carbon with transition metals such as iron and [[Cobalt|cobalt]] catalyzed their formation. Applications under study include [[Composite material|composite materials]] and [[Electronics|electronics]], though purification and toxicity remain challenges.

Organochlorine compound, CCl₄, a dense, nonflammable, colorless liquid with a sweet [[Chloroform|chloroform]]-like odor. Formerly used in fire extinguishers, as a precursor to refrigerants and as a cleaning agent, it has been phased out because of environmental and safety concerns. High exposure can affect the [[Central nervous system|central nervous system]] and degenerate the liver and kidneys, and prolonged exposure can be fatal. Its atmospheric lifetime exceeds 25 years, and it is regulated under the Montreal Protocol.

Italian [[Pasta|pasta]] dish made with cured pork, hard cheese, eggs, salt and [[Black pepper]]. Typical of the [[Lazio]] region, it took its modern form and name in the mid-20th century. Guanciale, a cured pork jowl, is traditional, though pancetta is used in some variations and smoked bacon is a common substitute outside Italy. Pecorino romano is the usual cheese, though some versions use Parmesan or Grana Padano. Spaghetti is the most common pasta, but bucatini and rigatoni are also used.

Salt or ester of carbonic acid (H₂CO₃), containing the carbonate ion, CO₃²⁻. The term also describes carbonation, raising carbonate and bicarbonate concentrations in water to make carbonated water and beverages. The most common carbonate minerals are [[Calcite|calcite]] (CaCO₃), the chief constituent of [[Limestone|limestone]] and the main component of mollusk shells and [[Coral|coral]] skeletons; dolomite (CaMg(CO₃)₂); and siderite (FeCO₃), an important [[Iron ore|iron ore]]. [[Sodium carbonate]] (Na₂CO₃) and potassium carbonate have been used since antiquity for cleaning, preservation and glassmaking. Carbonates are used in iron smelting, as raw materials for Portland cement and lime, and in ceramic glazes. New applications include thermal energy storage and use as catalysts and electrolytes in molten carbonate fuel cells.

Geologic period of the [[Paleozoic]] era, from 358.86 to 298.9 million years ago. Its name, from Latin for coal-bearing, refers to the coal beds formed worldwide at the time. Early [[Amphibian|amphibians]], such as temnospondyls, became dominant land vertebrates, and the period is sometimes called the Age of Amphibians. Amniotes appeared late in the period, and [[Insect|insects]], many of them flying, radiated. Forests and swamps covered the land. Later glaciations and mountain building accompanied the collision of continents to form [[Pangaea]].

Polar organic acid containing a carboxyl group, –C(=O)OH, attached to an R-group. Its general formula is R–COOH, where R is an organic group such as an alkyl or aryl group, or a hydrogen atom, as in [[Formic acid|formic acid]]. Carboxylic acids are generally weak acids that partially ionize in water; simple aliphatic examples have pKa values of about 3.75 to 4.82. Their boiling points are higher than those of hydrocarbons or [[Alcohol (chemistry)|alcohols]] of comparable molecular weight, because they form hydrogen-bonded dimers. [[Acetic acid|Acetic acid]] is the acid in vinegar, while [[Amino acid|amino acids]] and [[Fatty acid|fatty acids]] are essential biological molecules. Carboxylic acids are precursors to [[Ester|esters]] and amides and take part in the [[Citric acid|citric acid]] cycle.

Chemical, physical or biological agent promoting the development of cancer. Carcinogens include synthetic chemicals, natural substances, [[Ionizing radiation|ionizing]] and [[Ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] radiation, and viruses. Most act by creating mutations in [[DNA]] that disrupt the cell's control of growth. Some agents, such as polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, are activated into reactive metabolites in the body; others, including ultraviolet light, act directly on DNA. The latency period is often 10 to 40 years for solid tumors. The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies agents into four groups, from Group 1 (carcinogenic to humans) to Group 3 (not classifiable). Occupational exposure is a major source, with an estimated 666,000 annual fatalities worldwide from work-related cancers.

[[Spice]] made from the seed pods of several plants in the genera *Elettaria* and *Amomum*, in the ginger family Zingiberaceae. Both genera are native to the [[Indian subcontinent]] and [[Indonesia]]. Green cardamom pods are smaller and light green, while black cardamom pods are larger and dark brown. The first references to cardamom are found in [[Sumer]] and in [[Ayurveda]]. In the 21st century it is cultivated mainly in [[India]], Indonesia and [[Guatemala]], which is the leading exporter, with over 40% of global supply as of 2023. It flavors curries, baked goods and coffee, and has long been used as a digestive aid. Its essential oil is used in perfumes.

Sudden, unexpected cessation of effective heart function, also called sudden cardiac arrest. The heart stops beating or beats in a way that fails to produce a [[Pulse|pulse]], so blood flow to the brain and other organs falls, and brain cells begin to die within minutes. It is usually caused by an [[Arrhythmia|arrhythmia]], most often ventricular fibrillation or ventricular [[Tachycardia|tachycardia]]. Risk factors include age, cardiovascular disease and [[Coronary artery disease|coronary artery disease]]. Treatment aims to restore circulation quickly through cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), defibrillation or pacing. In the United States, about 535,000 cases occur annually according to 2015 American Heart Association guidelines, 61% of them outside a hospital.

Capital and largest city of [[Wales]] (pop., 2025: 381,516). Located in southeast Wales on the River Taff, it grew from a small town into a port for coal exported from the valleys in the 19th century. It was ranked as a city in 1905 and proclaimed capital of Wales in 1955. It is the eleventh largest city in the [[United Kingdom]], and its Cardiff Bay area contains the Senedd (Welsh Parliament). Cardiff is a major center of television and film production, including the 2005 revival of [[Doctor Who]], and is the most visited destination in Wales.

Italian-born Catholic prelate, diplomat and statesman. He was made a cardinal in 1641 and from 1642 until his death served as chief minister to [[Louis XIII]] and [[Louis XIV]] of France. He had entered French service under [[Cardinal Richelieu]], and as head of government for the regent Anne of Austria he also oversaw the young king's education. His diplomacy helped conclude the [[Thirty Years' War]] with the [[Peace of Westphalia]], whose principles of state sovereignty shaped later international law. He faced the Fronde revolts of 1648–1653. The Treaty of the Pyrenees (1659) added three provinces to France. He introduced Italian opera on a grand scale to Paris, assembled an art collection now partly in the [[Louvre]], and founded the Bibliothèque Mazarine, the first true public library in France.

French Catholic prelate and statesman, known as the Red Eminence. Made a cardinal in 1622, he became chief minister to [[Louis XIII]] in 1624 and held that office until his death, when he was succeeded by [[Cardinal Mazarin]]. He strengthened royal power by restraining the nobility and aimed to make France a centralized state. In foreign policy he sought to check the Habsburgs and secure French dominance in the [[Thirty Years' War]], subsidizing Protestant states such as the Swedish Empire and the Dutch Republic. He suppressed the [[Huguenots]] rebellions, founded the Académie Française in 1635 as the learned society responsible for the [[French language]], and founded the Compagnie des Cent-Associés (1627) to advance [[New France]]. His Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye (1632) returned [[Quebec City]] to French rule.

Any of the four main compass directions: north (N), east (E), south (S) and west (W). The intercardinal, or ordinal, directions northeast, southeast, southwest and northwest lie midway between them. Their azimuths, measured clockwise from north, are 0°, 90°, 180° and 270° for the cardinal directions, and 45°, 135°, 225° and 315° for the ordinal ones. The term comes from [[Latin]] cardo, meaning hinge or axis, reflecting their role as the basis for all other directions. East corresponds to the direction of sunrise, and the cardinal directions underpin systems such as [[Latitude]] and [[Longitude]].

Family of [[New World]] [[Passerine|passerine]] birds, including cardinals, grosbeaks and buntings, and tanager-like genera such as *Piranga*. Membership is defined by molecular studies rather than physical traits. Males of many species are brightly colored in red, yellow or blue, and most species are monogamous and nest in open cups. Most are arboreal, though the dickcissel is a ground-dwelling [[Prairie|prairie]] bird. The family comprises 56 species in 13 genera, ranging from southern [[Canada]] to northern [[Argentina]] and Chile. Most species are least concern on the IUCN Red List, but the Carrizal seedeater is endangered.
